title: Vietnam Won't Become the World's Factory, But It May Be the Last Confucian Emerging Market
dek: Vietnam's GDP per capita is only $3,700, equivalent to China in 2003. Its opportunity isn't to replicate China's full industrial chain, but to pick a few industries and reach developed-country levels, the way the Four Asian Tigers did.
why: Medium information density. The first half is a personal migration story; the second half, on Vietnam's economic structure, north-south differences and business risks, is more valuable for judgment.
who: Founders and investors watching Southeast Asia expansion, manufacturing relocation and emerging-market investment, plus anyone considering living or working in Vietnam.
skip: The opening Vietnamese greeting and the north-south accent comparison can be skipped, roughly the first 5 minutes.

points.h: Vietnam is the last untapped Confucian market
points.body: The core logic behind Yang Fan's judgment on Vietnam's opportunity: most markets shaped by Confucian culture — Japan, the Four Asian Tigers, mainland China — are already well developed, and Vietnam is the last emerging market that hasn't yet developed. He sums up this cultural sphere as ‘eating with chopsticks’, underpinned by Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism. The key to this judgment isn't the culture itself, but the behavioral traits the culture produces: a hardworking and pragmatic people, emphasis on education, and a pursuit of worldly success. These traits are not common in other Southeast Asian countries — Indonesia, for instance, is the largest Muslim country, and Thailand is Theravada Buddhist, where the pursuit is more about religious fulfillment.

points.h: Vietnam will not become the world's factory
points.body: Yang Fan states plainly that Vietnam will not become the world's factory, because its size decides it. Vietnam's total population is just over 98 million, more than Germany, more than South Korea, with an area about the same as Japan. China could develop a full industrial chain because of its land area, population size and earlier accumulation — Vietnam doesn't have these conditions. He thinks Vietnam is more likely to develop in the direction of the Four Asian Tigers, picking a few industries the way South Korea did — Samsung's electronics, Hyundai Motors, shipbuilding, high-precision chemicals — and if it can develop several of them well, it could become a developed country. But he also stresses this requires the right timing, advantages and people, a kind of historical accident.

points.h: People matter more than timing or geography
points.body: Yang Fan breaks Vietnam's development over the past decade into timing, geography and people, and argues people matter most — meaning Confucian culture. He gives several concrete supports: Vietnam ranks in the top 12 globally for engineering graduates; Vietnam is the world's second-largest IT outsourcing hub after India; Vietnam's female employment rate is 10 points higher than China's; the median age is just over 30, very young. On the high female employment rate, he speculates it may be related to war — male mortality during wartime was very high, women had to do everything in the villages, and became the backbone of economic development.

points.h: Men do big things, and fighting a war is a big thing
points.body: There's a Vietnamese proverb: men do big things. Yang Fan explains: what is a big thing? Fighting a war is a big thing. This has led to Vietnamese men today being somewhat more languid, while women, besides working, also take care of the family, and are extremely hardworking. He also mentions another feature of Vietnamese culture: it only extends to China's Ming dynasty, and never experienced the Qing dynasty's suppression of Han culture, so there were no restrictions on women's social status like foot binding. At the same time he stresses that Vietnamese men are very resilient — the only people in the world who beat the US military are the Han Chinese and Vietnam's ethnic Kinh majority.

points.h: Vietnam has four slims, and land is permanent-use rights
points.body: Yang Fan says Vietnam has four slims: a slim country, slim pho, slim women in ao dai, slim houses. Houses are slim because the tax system is like the Netherlands', taxing by the width of the house's facade, so people like to build narrow and deep, and build upward. The key difference is that land is permanent-use rights — when a new family member arrives you can build another floor on top, and the ground floor can be rented to a shop. So for locals life is quite easy, and there's no need to buy another house. Foreigners have been able to buy since July 2015, but only apartments, not land — and what appreciates fastest in Vietnam is land.

points.h: Vietnam is safe, but low-level officials will skim benefits
points.body: Yang Fan says Vietnam is a very safe country, tied to its Confucian cultural foundation. He gives the example of Hanoi: if someone on the street dares to do wrong to anyone, a bunch of Hanoi's ‘Chaoyang grandmas’ rush over to beat that person up — the moral demands are very high. Ho Chi Minh City has motorcycle phone-snatching, but Hanoi doesn't. On the business environment, Vietnam is very similar to China: the government welcomes foreign investment, but low-level officials hold approval power and want to skim benefits from companies. Compared with the West, Vietnam is not so rule-of-law, it's still officialdom-centered, and also a society of personal connections — to do business well you have to cultivate relationships with all kinds of people.

points.h: The China model hits a size ceiling in Vietnam
points.body: Yang Fan gives a concrete example: a Chinese luxury brand contacted his friend in Vietnam, planning to open 500 stores in Vietnam in five years, and asked if it was possible. His friend thought about it and said, 500 — you'd be doing well to open two. Vietnam is one north, one south — one Hanoi, one Ho Chi Minh City. Because China is so large, any vertical can be done at great scale, but Vietnam's size is much smaller. He also mentions that southern Vietnam is more Southeast Asian — people won't work overtime, and the pace of getting things done is unexpectedly slow. This is the pit Chinese companies most easily fall into when they go to Vietnam with Chinese habitual thinking.

points.h: Don't only go to Ho Chi Minh City — you have to pay respects in Hanoi
points.body: Yang Fan's advice for Chinese companies: manufacturing firms need to find a good industrial park — Vietnam has roughly 500 industrial parks from north to south, but only about half may be operating, and quality varies. For other companies, including fairly large Chinese internet firms, the mistake is that they all only come to Ho Chi Minh City, because Ho Chi Minh is the economic center, was formerly called Saigon, and is more famous — but they neglect Hanoi. Hanoi is the capital, equivalent to China's Beijing, and many matters of paying respects have to be done in Hanoi. He also warns that many people come over, take one look and feel it's very much like China, but in actual operations you must absolutely not be kidnapped by this ‘very much alike’ — there are many subtle places that are very different.

quotes.text: I think Vietnam won't become the world's factory. As for the world's factory — worldwide, would you say Japan is the world's factory? Japan isn't either. Is South Korea? South Korea isn't either. It's decided by their size.
Vietnam has a very interesting proverb: men do big things. So what is a big thing? Fighting a war is a big thing. So this has led to Vietnamese men today being somewhat more languid.

My friend thought about it and said, 500 stores — you'd be doing well to open two. Vietnam is one north, one south — one Hanoi, one Ho Chi Minh City. Then how do you open them? The size is just much smaller.

Some Grab drivers, sometimes you'll see them lying on their motorbikes, sunbathing, quite happy. They don't want to take that many jobs. When they get off work, they'll go to the river with a little line and catch a very big fish — a fish this big — and go home.

Many people come over, take one look and feel it's very much like China — it really is very much alike. But in actual operations, you must absolutely not be kidnapped by these feelings of being very much alike.

If there's no traffic jam, sitting on the back of a motorbike, whether it's the wind blowing in the daytime sun or the evening breeze at night, that feeling is very, very good — a very happy moment. You don't feel that kind of moment in Hong Kong.
I once made an inappropriate analogy: I said that in the night breeze of Saigon, you can smell the scent of hormones. It's really there, it's really there.
